summary: Describes a cryptographic authentication mechanism for the Babel routing protocol, using message authentication codes, with provisions to avoid replayed messages. It obsoletes RFC 7298.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 8967 adds message authentication to Babel routing packets so a router can reject forged routing information. Packet counters and fresh indices help detect replay, and a nonce challenge checks a peer after its counter state is lost; the mechanism uses shared keys and does not encrypt traffic.

questions: what is a babel pc tlv
how does babel stop replay attacks
subtitle: Authenticates Babel routing packets and uses counters and challenges to limit replay.

tldr.problem: Without authentication, a Babel router may accept forged or replayed packets that change routes or disrupt the network.
tldr.mechanism: Routers append keyed message authentication codes and a packet counter with a fresh index; a challenge and reply verify a peer when its counter state is unknown or reset.
tldr.outcome: The mechanism supports shared-key authentication, replay protection, incremental deployment, and key rotation, but not confidentiality or asymmetric keys. RFC 8967 obsoletes RFC 7298 and is updated by RFC 9467.

today: RFC 8967 is a Proposed Standard that obsoletes RFC 7298 and is updated by RFC 9467.

sections.title: Authenticating Babel Packets
sections.content:
Babel normally trusts the information in received packets. An attacker could forge a route, send a malformed packet, or replay an older packet to redirect traffic or disrupt routing.

This extension adds cryptographic authentication to Babel packets for both unicast and multicast communication. It assumes that interfaces on the same link share a small set of symmetric keys and are equally trusted.
sections.plainLanguage: Without packet authentication, a router cannot tell whether a routing update came from an authorized neighbor. This extension lets neighbors check that packets were created by someone who knows a shared key.

sections.title: Computing the Message Authentication Code
sections.content:
A sender calculates a Message Authentication Code (MAC) over a pseudo-header and the Babel packet, then adds the result as a MAC TLV in the packet trailer. The pseudo-header includes source and destination IP addresses and UDP ports.

HMAC-SHA256 is required for implementation. Keyed BLAKE2s with 128-bit digests is recommended, and a receiver accepts a packet only if a computed MAC matches one carried in the packet.
sections.plainLanguage: The MAC is a keyed check over the packet and its network addresses. A receiver computes the check with its shared key and discards a packet if none of the checks match.

sections.title: Counters and Fresh Indices
sections.content:
Each authenticated packet includes a Packet Counter (PC) and an Index in a PC TLV. The sender increases the counter for each packet; if it overflows or may have reset, the sender chooses a fresh index.

A receiver accepts packets only when their counter is greater than the last accepted counter for the same index. If the index is new or unknown, the receiver does not accept ordinary packets until the sender proves freshness through a challenge exchange.
sections.plainLanguage: The counter lets a receiver reject packets it has already seen or that arrived out of order. A new index signals that counter history may have changed, so the receiver asks the sender to prove it is live.

sections.title: Challenge and Reply
sections.content:
The receiver sends a Challenge Request containing a nonce that it has not used before. A peer that knows the shared key returns the same nonce in a MAC-protected Challenge Reply with its current packet counter.

The receiver accepts that reply only when its nonce matches an unexpired challenge. Challenges and replies are rate-limited to reduce the work an attacker can trigger with replayed packets.
sections.plainLanguage: A random challenge asks the peer to prove it can answer now, not just replay an old packet. The peer echoes the challenge in an authenticated reply, allowing the receiver to trust its fresh counter value.

sections.title: Scope and Key Management
sections.content:
This mechanism provides authentication and replay defenses, but not confidentiality or asymmetric keying. The security properties depend on a MAC that resists forgery and on indices and nonces never being reused with the relevant keys.

Keys should be difficult to guess, and implementations must expire per-neighbor counter state within a finite time. The protocol supports staged deployment by first accepting unauthenticated packets while sending authenticated ones, and supports key rotation by temporarily using both keys.
sections.plainLanguage: The protocol checks who sent a packet but does not hide its contents. Secure operation also depends on strong shared keys and never reusing the values that identify counters and challenges.
